title: Signs of a Failing Shower Pan and Hidden Damage Under the Tile | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: How to recognize a failing shower pan, what happens to the subfloor under the tile, and why the damage often shows up in the next room first.
h1: The Signs of a Failing Shower Pan, & the Damage Happening Under the Tile
intro: You have probably walked past it a hundred times without letting yourself stop on it. A grout line that stays dark hours after anyone showered. A baseboard in the hallway that has started to curl away from the wall, on the other side of the bathroom, for no reason you can name. Maybe a smell that comes and goes, faint enough that you talk yourself out of it. Nothing has broken. Nothing is leaking in the way leaks are supposed to leak, no puddle, no drip, no sound. And yet something keeps nagging, and you keep cleaning the same spot, and the spot keeps coming back. That gap between knowing something is wrong and being able to point at it is genuinely hard to sit in. It is not paranoia. Slow shower pan failures are built to hide, and the not-knowing is part of how they work.

sections.heading: The tile is not what keeps water in the shower
sections.body:
Most people assume the tile and grout are the waterproofing. They are not. Tile is a wear surface, and grout is porous by design. The part that holds water is underneath: a membrane or a pre-formed pan liner that sits below the mortar bed, sloped toward the drain, turned up the walls a few inches at the curb and corners. Water passes through the grout constantly, every shower, by design. It lands on that membrane and runs to weep holes in the drain assembly, and you never know it happened.

So a shower pan does not usually fail the way a pipe fails. It fails at a seam, a corner fold, a nail that was driven through the liner during framing, a curb that was never fully sealed, or a drain flange whose weep holes packed solid with mortar years ago. The failure is small, and the water that gets past it is small, but it arrives every single day the shower is used. That is why the visible damage almost never lines up with a single event you can remember.

sections.heading: The signs, in roughly the order they tend to appear
sections.body: None of these prove a pan has failed on its own. Together, especially two or three at once, they are worth paying attention to.

cards.heading: Grout and caulk that will not stay put
cards.body: Grout that keeps cracking or crumbling in the same corner, or caulk at the wall-to-floor joint that peels back within months of being redone, usually means movement underneath. A mortar bed that has taken on water softens and shifts slightly with weight, and the brittle surface on top is the first thing to give.

cards.heading: Loose, hollow, or shifting tile
cards.body: Tap along the shower floor with a knuckle or the handle of a screwdriver. A solid bed sounds dull and dense. A hollow, drummy sound means the mortar has separated from the substrate, often because water has been sitting in it. Tiles that rock slightly under a heel are further along than that.

cards.heading: Discoloration that returns after cleaning
cards.body: A stain that comes back within days of scrubbing is not surface mildew, it is water moving through from behind. Same with grout lines that dry noticeably slower than the ones next to them, or a persistent damp ring at the base of the curb.

cards.heading: Damage in the next room, not the bathroom
cards.body: This is the one that confuses people most. Water follows the slope of the framing, not the walls of the shower. Cupping or dark edges on hardwood in the adjacent hallway, a soft spot in the closet floor that backs the shower, or paint bubbling on the far side of a shared wall are all classic shower pan symptoms.

cards.heading: A smell you cannot locate
cards.body: Musty odor that gets stronger when the bathroom door has been closed, or when the HVAC kicks on, points to something growing on wet organic material inside the assembly: framing, subfloor, paper facing on drywall. If it fades when you open a window and returns, it is coming from inside the structure.

cards.heading: Staining on a ceiling below
cards.body: On a second-floor shower, a brown ring or a sagging patch on the ceiling underneath is the end of a long process, not the start of one. By the time water has soaked through a subfloor and a ceiling cavity, the framing between them has already been wet for a long time.

sections.heading: What the water has been doing while you were not looking
sections.body:
Under a failed pan, the mortar bed acts like a sponge. It holds water against the plywood or OSB subfloor for days at a time, and wood that stays above roughly 20 percent moisture content will begin to break down and support mold growth. In Arizona this surprises people, because the dry climate outside does nothing for a wet cavity that is sealed under tile and never gets airflow.

From there it moves outward along the path of least resistance. It wicks into the bottom plate of the framed wall, then up through the drywall behind the tile backer. It travels along floor joists and shows up somewhere with no plumbing in it at all. On a slab foundation it spreads laterally under the mortar bed and comes out at the base of the far wall. In every version, the tile you are looking at stays fine long after the structure behind it stopped being fine, which is exactly why the discovery so often feels sudden when it has been anything but.

That is also why re-grouting and re-caulking usually buys weeks rather than years. Sealing the top of an assembly that is already holding water does not dry it out. It just makes the surface look correct for a while longer.

sections.heading: How the problem actually gets confirmed and resolved
sections.body: Confirming a pan failure means getting behind the finish surface. A moisture meter and a thermal camera can map where water is sitting without opening anything, which usually shows a pattern that traces back to a corner, a curb, or the drain. Sometimes the shower is flood-tested: the drain is plugged, the pan is filled to just below the curb, and the level is watched for a day while someone checks below for movement. That is how you separate a pan failure from a supply line, a leaking valve, or a drain connection. When the assembly is opened, the work splits in two. The wet materials have to come out and the cavity has to be dried and treated before anything is closed back up, which is the mitigation side of water damage restoration. Then the shower has to be rebuilt: new pan or membrane, new backer, new tile, and whatever framing, drywall, flooring, or trim came out with it, which is reconstruction and rebuild work. Homeowners are often caught off guard that these are two different phases, and that skipping straight to new tile over a cavity that was never dried is how the same problem returns in the same corner. faqs.q: Can a shower pan leak without any visible water in the bathroom
faqs.a: Yes, and that is the usual case. The membrane sits below the tile and mortar, so water that gets past it goes into the floor assembly rather than out onto the bathroom floor. It commonly appears first as damaged flooring, trim, or paint in an adjacent room or on a ceiling below.

faqs.q: Will re-grouting or re-caulking fix a failing shower pan
faqs.a: Not if the pan itself has failed. Grout and caulk are surface materials, not the waterproofing layer. Redoing them can slow water entry at a cracked joint, but it cannot repair a torn liner, an unsealed corner, or clogged weep holes at the drain, and it seals moisture into an assembly that is already wet.

faqs.q: How do I tell a shower pan leak from a supply line leak
faqs.a: Timing is the biggest clue. A supply line under pressure leaks whether or not anyone is using the shower, so the wet area grows continuously. A pan failure only lets water through while the shower is running and draining, so the damage tends to worsen in steps after use. A flood test and moisture mapping confirm which one it is.

faqs.q: Does the whole shower have to come out
faqs.a: Sometimes, and sometimes not. It depends on where the failure is and how far the moisture has traveled. A pan liner cannot be patched in place under a finished floor, so the shower floor and lower walls usually come out, but the extent beyond that is determined by moisture readings in the framing, subfloor, and adjacent rooms rather than by guesswork.
